The EDVI Act sounds compassionate, but federalizing children’s vision care is a recipe for bureaucratic bloat. We’ve seen this playbook before—Washington creates a “first-ever” program, then layers it with grants, data collection mandates, and interagency collaborations that drain resources. The bill’s own summary admits it’ll establish HRSA grants and CDC surveillance systems, which means taxpayer dollars funding administrative overhead instead of direct care.

States already manage vision screening through schools and Medicaid—why add another layer of federal control? This isn’t about helping kids; it’s about expanding the nanny state.

Real solutions empower parents and local providers, not D.C. middlemen skimming funds for “technical assistance centers” and equity audits. Fix existing programs before launching new ones.

The real cost isn’t just dollars—it’s lost accountability and diluted care; see the evidence laid bare: https://t.co/OoybfehxcB

AI’s potential in healthcare is real—but let’s not pretend D.C. bureaucrats are the ones driving innovation. The Health Tech Investment Act (S.1399) proves the swamp’s priorities: Section 2(a)(1) mandates Medicare pay for algorithm-based services using FDA-cleared devices, yet Section 2(b) codifies CMS’s “software as a service” policy that’s ripe for abuse.

We’re talking about Medicare Advantage plans already weaponizing AI to deny claims while taxpayers foot the bill for redundant systems. Innovation thrives when government gets out of the way—not when it layers subscription fees and invoice price mandates on providers.

Heard any hearings about slashing FDA’s 20-year-old regulatory frameworks? Exactly. Priorities.

Doubling funding for AI-driven childhood cancer research sounds noble—but where’s the accountability? The CCDI’s budget surge to $100M must prioritize real-world results over bureaucratic bloat. Taxpayers deserve transparency: How much goes to AI contractors vs. actual treatments?

Trump’s original 2019 database was a breakthrough, but doubling budgets without audits risks repeating NIH’s history of overspending on “innovation” that rarely reaches patients. Track every dollar, demand measurable outcomes, and cut middlemen.

Hope matters, but efficiency saves lives.
